4852621.fragment: Fizz and Red bank oysters. Effect on the sexual. Aphrodis. He was in the Red Bank this morning.

range.content: Fizz and Red bank oysters. Effect on the sexual. Aphrodis. He was in the Red Bank this morning.

4852621.twitter_share_message: “This is another great example for Joyces technique of visualizing his characters chains of thoug…” —@Genius

children: This is another great example for Joyces technique of visualizing his characters chains of thought. Though it is just four short lines, the allusions are rather complex and challenge the readers attention and background knowledge.
(1) A region famous for its oysters are the red-bank beds in County Clare, situated on the west coast of Ireland (see: Gifford:
Ulysses Annotated
, 8.865-66). Hence, Bloom is referencing fizz (champagne) and red-bank oysters as a delicacy, contrasting it with the “garbage, sewage they [oysters] feed on”.
(2) Oysters are rumored to be aphrodisiacs (“Aphrodis”). Bloom is consequently lead into thinking about their “effect on the sexual”.

(3) The Red Bank Restaurant (“the Red Bank”) is a restaurant in Dublin, named after the famous oysters being served there. It was first referenced in Chapter 6 when Bloom and his companions saw Blazen Boylan, the man Molly is having an affair with, standing in front of its entrance.

This allows us to fully understand Blooms train of thought. His meditations on food lead him to thinking about oysters, particularily about red-bank oysters and their rumored “effect on the sexual”. “Red-bank”, in turn, reminds him of the restaurant, which brings up seeing Boylan there earlier in the day. The thought of him eating oysters with all its sexual connotations, especially in light of the scheduled meeting of Boylan and Molly later that day (compare Chapter 4), serves as a painful reminder of the adultery and further intensifies the worries that haunt Bloom all day long.

4857874.fragment: No June has no ar no oysters. But there are people like things high. Tainted game.

range.content: no June has no ar no oysters. But there are people like things high. Tainted game.

4857874.twitter_share_message: “Since the 18th century, oysterfishing was prohibited in France, the United Kingdom and the Unite…” —@Genius

children: Since the 18th century, oysterfishing was prohibited in France, the United Kingdom and the United States during the months without the letter “r” in their names (i.e. May, June, July and August). These close seasons were instituted to combat the decline in oyster populations due to constant overfishing.
As
Ulysses
is set in June and “June has no ar”, Bloom concludes that there are currently no oysters being served.

The next two sentences (starting with “But there are…”), however, show Bloom sharing the widely held belief that the “r-rule” was originally implemented because of a lack of reliable refrigeration. After noting “no ar no oysters”, he is thus led into thinking about spoiled goods (“things high”, “tainted game”), continuing his train of thought.
It is worth noting that connoisseurs are adhering to the “r-rule” up until today, even though both the refigerating and breeding problems have been solved for a long time.
For further information about the “r-rule”,
click here
(in German).

8816755.twitter_share_message: “‘Cherchez la femme’ is sometimes mistakenly thought to refer to men’s attempts to pursue romanti…” —@Genius

children: ‘Cherchez la femme’ is sometimes mistakenly thought to refer to men’s attempts to pursue romantic liaisons with women. In fact, the phrase, which is occasionally used in its loose English translation ‘look for the woman’, expresses the idea that the source of any given problem involving a man is liable to be a woman.

The expression was coined by Alexandre Dumas (père) in the novel The Mohicans of Paris, 1864, in the form of ‘cherchons la femme’. In John Latey’s 1878 English translation, Dumas' detective, Monsieur Jackal, concludes that a woman must have been involved in the crime being investigated:
“Where’s the woman? Seek her.”
His opinion was later confirmed by a colleague:
“Ah! Monsieur Jackal, you were right when you said, ‘Seek the woman.’”

Cormac is said to have turned to Christianity some years before his death.
